Early nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) versus
early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) for preterm
infants
Brigitte Lemyre1, Marc-Olivier Deguise2,3, Paige Benson3, Haresh Kirpalani4, Osayame A Ekhaguere5, Peter G Davis6
1Division of Neonatology, Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario, Ottawa, Canada. 2Dept. of Pediatrics, Children's Hospital of Eastern

Contact: Brigitte Lemyre, blemyre@toh.ca.
Editorial group: Cochrane Neonatal Group.
Publication status and date: New search for studies and content updated (conclusions changed), published in Issue 7, 2023.
Citation: Lemyre B, Deguise M-O, Benson P, Kirpalani H, Ekhaguere OA, Davis PG. Early nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation
(NIPPV) versus early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) for preterm infants. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
2023, Issue 7. Art. No.: CD005384. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD005384.pub3.
Copyright © 2023 The Cochrane Collaboration. Published by John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
A B S T R A C T
Background
Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) is a strategy to maintain positive airway pressure throughout the respiratory cycle
through the application of a bias flow of respiratory gas to an apparatus attached to the nose. Early treatment with NCPAP is associated
with decreased risk of mechanical ventilation exposure and might reduce chronic lung disease. Nasal intermittent positive pressure
ventilation (NIPPV) is a form of noninvasive ventilation delivered through the same nasal interface during which patients are exposed to
short inflations, along with background end-expiratory pressure.
Objectives
To examine the risks and benefits of early (within the first six hours afer birth) NIPPV versus early NCPAP for preterm infants at risk of or
with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).
Primary endpoints are respiratory failure and the need for intubated ventilatory support during the first week of life. Secondary endpoints
include the incidence of mortality, chronic lung disease (CLD) (oxygen therapy at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age), pneumothorax, duration
of respiratory support, duration of oxygen therapy, and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH).
Search methods
Searches were conducted in January 2023 in CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Dissertation Abstracts. The reference lists
of related systematic reviews and of studies selected for inclusion were also searched.
Selection criteria
We considered all randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials. Eligible studies compared NIPPV versus NCPAP treatment, starting
within six hours afer birth in preterm infants (< 37 weeks' gestational age (GA)).
Data collection and analysis
We collected and analyzed data using the recommendations of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group.

Main results
We included 17 trials, enrolling 1958 infants in this review. NIPPV likely reduces the rate of respiratory failure (risk ratio (RR) 0.65, 95%
confidence interval (CI) 0.54 to 0.78; risk diference (RD) -0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.05; 17 RCTs, 1958 infants; moderate-certainty evidence)
and needing endotracheal tube ventilation (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.81; RD -0.07, 95% CI -0.11 to -0.04; 16 RCTs; 1848 infants; moderate-
certainty evidence) amongst infants treated with early NIPPV compared with early NCPAP.
The meta-analysis demonstrated that NIPPV may reduce the risk of developing CLD compared to CPAP (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.92; 12
RCTs, 1284 infants; low-certainty evidence) slightly. NIPPV may result in little to no diference in mortality (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.10; 17
RCTs; 1958 infants; I2 of 0%; low-certainty evidence), the incidence of pneumothorax (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.41; 16 RCTs; 1674 infants; I2
of 0%; low-certainty evidence), and rates of severe IVH (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.79; 8 RCTs; 977 infants; I2 of 0%; low-certainty evidence).
Authors' conclusions
When applied within six hours afer birth, NIPPV likely reduces the risk of respiratory failure and the need for intubation and endotracheal
tube ventilation in very preterm infants (GA 28 weeks and above) with respiratory distress syndrome or at risk for RDS. It may also decrease
the rate of CLD slightly. However, most trials enrolled infants with a gestational age of approximately 28 to 32 weeks with an overall mean
gestational age of around 30 weeks. As such, the results of this review may not apply to extremely preterm infants that are most at risk
of needing mechanical ventilation or developing CLD. Additional studies are needed to confirm these results and to assess the safety of
NIPPV compared with NCPAP alone in a larger patient population.
P L A I N   L A N G U A G E   S U M M A R Y
Early nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) versus early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) for
preterm infants
Review question
Does NIPPV confer greater short-term and long-term benefits without harm to preterm infants with or at risk of respiratory distress
compared with NCPAP?
Background
Nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) may increase the efectiveness of nasal continuous positive airway pressure
(NCPAP) in preterm babies who have respiratory dificulties or are at risk of such dificulties. Preterm babies with breathing problems
ofen require help from a machine (ventilator) that provides regular breaths through a tube in the windpipe. Pediatricians caring for these
preterm infants try to avoid the use of ventilators, as they can damage the growing immature or premature lung. NCPAP and NIPPV are
ways of supporting babies' breathing in a less invasive way - the tubes are shorter and go only to the back of the nose, thereby causing less
damage to the lungs. NCPAP and NIPPV may be used early afer birth to reduce the number of babies needing the assistance of a ventilator
for breathing. NCPAP provides steady pressure to the back of the nose that is transmitted to the lungs, helping the baby breathe more
comfortably. NIPPV provides the same support but also adds some breaths through the ventilator.
Study characteristics
We searched scientific databases for studies comparing NCPAP with NIPPV in preterm infants (born before 37 completed weeks of
pregnancy) who needed respiratory support shortly afer birth. We looked at the need for a breathing tube and long-term side efects.
Key results
We found 17 trials (enrolling 1958 infants) comparing NCPAP with NIPPV. When applied within six hours afer birth, NIPPV likely reduces
the risk of respiratory failure and the need for intubation and endotracheal tube ventilation in very preterm infants (gestational age of
28 weeks and above) with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) or at risk for RDS. It may also decrease the rate of chronic lung disease
slightly. Compared to NCPAP, NIPPV may result in little to no diference on the risk of dying, developing an air leak in the thoracic cage, or
a severe brain bleed. However, there was a lack of data for the most premature infants that are born at less than 28 weeks of gestational
age. Additional studies are needed to determine how NIPPV can be best delivered to infants. The evidence is up-to-date to January 2023.
Certainty of the evidence
The overall certainty of the studies included in this review was moderate to low.

B A C K G R O U N D
Preterm infants are at risk for respiratory distress in the perinatal
period. This is usually due to their developing lungs and a
surfactant deficiency consequent to their immaturity. This state
of surfactant deficiency is called respiratory distress syndrome. As
such, preterm infants ofen require respiratory support to sustain
their breathing.
Description of the condition
Because of their immature lung, preterm infants may go into
respiratory failure leading to the need for mechanical ventilation.
This is the primary outcome of this review. This is an important
outcome because of its close linkage to the development of
chronic lung disease of prematurity. The immature surfactant-
deficient lung is susceptible to injury from exposure to mechanical
ventilators (Kalikkot Thekkeveedu 2017; Philip 1975). Lung injury
is due to the combined efects of volutrauma, barotrauma,
atelectotrauma, rheotrauma, and biotrauma, culminating in the
arrest of pulmonary development – the new chronic lung
disease (CLD), or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) (Donn 2006;
Dreyfuss 1998; Jobe 2011). CLD is the most common serious
morbidity amongst preterm infants. Originally defined as the
need for supplemental oxygen at 28 days of life, over time, the
definition evolved to the need for supplemental oxygen at 36
weeks' post-gestational age. CLD is associated with an increased
risk of many cardiovascular abnormalities, such as progressive
pulmonary hypertension (due to hypoxia and vasoconstriction
in the pulmonary vasculature), systemic hypertension, and lef
ventricular hypertrophy. It is important to note that, whereas the
survival of extremely low birth weight infants has increased over
the years, rates of CLD have stayed relatively constant despite
improving technology. To prevent these short- and long-term
adverse efects, clinicians strive to avoid or limit mechanical
ventilator exposure.
Description of the intervention
Noninvasive ventilation in spontaneously breathing preterm
infants is an established method of assisted ventilation.
Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) and nasal
intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) are two widely
applied modalities.
The benefits of NCPAP rely on the delivery of continuous distending
pressure to the lungs without an endotracheal tube (Morley 1999).
The distending pressure maintains functional residual capacity
by reducing elastic, flow, and inertial resistance properties of
the respiratory system, and stabilizes the compliant chest wall.
NCPAP is generated by conventional ventilators, bubble circuits,
or continuous positive airway (CPAP) drivers and can be delivered
to the patient by face mask, nasal mask, nasopharyngeal tube,
or nasal prongs. Since first described in the 1970s (Gregory 1971),
NCPAP has been used as a strategy for avoiding endotracheal tube
ventilation, thereby minimizing the risk of CLD. Used afer birth
in preterm infants in respiratory distress, NCPAP reduces the risk
of needing mechanical ventilation, but the efect size is small.
Moreover, a systematic review of trials of NCPAP versus intubation
as primary respiratory support in infants 24 to 26 weeks' gestation
showed a 45% to 50% NCPAP failure rate (Schmölzer 2013). Large
national registry data indicates a 21% NCPAP failure rate in infants
29 to 32 weeks' gestation (Dargaville 2016).
Like NCPAP, NIPPV provides continuous distending pressure; but
difers by superimposing a cycled peak inspiratory pressure (PIP)
over the baseline CPAP. NIPPV may be delivered by nasal mask
or prongs, which may be short or long, single or binasal. NIPPV
devices are generally classified in terms of the level of PIP they
generate and their ability to synchronize the cycled PIPs. However,
a problem is how efectively they may synchronize with a patient’s
spontaneous breathing (Owen 2016). With bilevel NIPPV, cycled
PIPs are 2 to 3 cm H20 above the positive end-expiratory pressure.
In contrast, ventilator NIPPV PIPs are similar to those used during
invasive ventilation. All ventilators can provide NIPPV; however,
synchronization requires special sensors that are not available on
all ventilators. Current methods of synchronization are subject to
the location in which it is used and difering agency regulations.
It includes (1) pneumatic capsules that detect abdominal wall
movement, (2) airflow sensors located at the patient-ventilator
interface, and (3) neurally adjusted ventilator assist (NAVA), which
utilizes diaphragmatic electromyogram signals (Owen 2016). The
use of NIPPV dates back to the 1970s (Helmrath 1970; Llewellyn
1970), but its association with severe complications initially limited
its adoption (Garland 1985). Better devices and patient interfaces
now exist, and the risk of major complications is substantially
lower (Owen 2016). Whether these additional features will result
in less need for endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilator
exposure is the objective of this review.
How the intervention might work
The peak inspiratory pressure generated with NIPPV is presumed
to be transmitted to the alveoli, maintaining functional residual
capacity while generating a tidal volume (Owen 2007; Owen
2016). However, observational data do not consistently validate
these results (Moretti 1999; Owen 2010; Owen 2011; Ryan 1989).
The only consistent finding is that NIPPV, regardless of device,
generates a higher mean airway pressure than NCPAP (Owen 2010;
Owen 2011). This may indicate why NIPPV reduces asynchronous
thoracoabdominal motion, perhaps as a result of reduced tube
resistance or better stabilization of the chest wall, or both
(Kiciman 1998). Other possible mechanisms of action include
pharyngeal inflation, triggering of the Head's paradoxical reflex,
and amelioration of apneic events. However, the results are
disparate when assessed clinically (Gizzi 2015; Pantalitschka 2009).
NIPPV may decrease the need for intubation and endotracheal tube
ventilation and their associated risks. To evaluate the eficacy of
NIPPV, these potential benefits should be weighed against the risks
associated with delivering positive pressure to the upper airway,
pharynx, and esophagus. Potential risks of NIPPV include nasal
septal injury and gastrointestinal perforation (Garland 1985).
Why it is important to do this review
Avoiding or reducing time spent on invasive ventilation is a goal of
treatment for all preterm infants. This review seeks to determine
whether NIPPV or NCPAP is a better primary mode of nasal
ventilation to prevent respiratory failure, the need for intubation,
and the development of CLD, without causing harm such as air
leak or intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). In doing so, we seek
to provide bedside clinicians with the best available evidence
regarding their choice of non-invasive support and aid in resource
allocation for preterm infants with respiratory distress in the first
six hours afer birth.

O B J E C T I V E S
To examine the risks and benefits of early (within the first six hours
afer birth) NIPPV versus early NCPAP alone for preterm infants at
risk of or with respiratory distress syndrome.
Primary endpoints are respiratory failure and the need for
intubated ventilatory support during the first week of life.
Secondary endpoints include the incidence of mortality, chronic
lung disease (CLD) (oxygen therapy at 36 weeks' postmenstrual
age), air leaks, duration of respiratory support, duration of oxygen
therapy, and intraventricular hemorrhage.
M E T H O D S
Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of studies
We considered randomized and quasi-randomized trials for
inclusion. Cross-over trials were considered for inclusion only if
interim data was available prior to cross-over.
Types of participants
We included studies that enrolled newly born preterm infants
at less than six hours of age. For this protocol, we defined
preterm infants as those born at less than 37 weeks' gestational
age. We included infants who received surfactant therapy even if
the duration of endotracheal intubation was short (for example,
INtubate, SURfactant, Extubate (INSURE)), and if the application of
NIPPV or NCPAP occurred before six hours afer birth.
The population of preterm infants included those at risk
of respiratory distress syndrome (which becomes increasingly
prevalent with decreasing gestational age) as well as those who
presented with RDS. Both groups were included as their distinction
is not clear in the literature. For example, many patients at risk
will eventually develop RDS and those may not be separable from
patients who don't, especially in the lowest gestational ages where
most patients are expected to develop the entity.
Types of interventions
Intermittent positive pressure ventilation provided by a ventilator
or a bilevel device and administered via the nasal route through
short nasal prongs or nasopharyngeal tubes versus NCPAP
delivered by the same methods. NIPPV included noninvasive
support delivered by a mechanical ventilator or a bilevel device in
a synchronized or non-synchronized way.
Types of outcome measures
Early respiratory outcomes and other pulmonary and safety
outcomes during admission were considered.
Primary outcomes
•
Respiratory failure: defined by respiratory acidosis, increased
oxygen requirement, or apnea that was frequent or severe,
leading to additional ventilatory support during the first week of
life.
◦ Need for endotracheal tube (ETT) ventilation (intermittent
positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) through an endotracheal
tube)
Respiratory failure and the need for endotracheal tube ventilation
are used as separate outcomes to diferentiate studies where
participants having respiratory failure may cross over to the
alternative intervention (from CPAP to NIPPV) without needing
intubation. This distinction may be present in some studies
available and may be more frequently reported to avoid
mechanical ventilation.
Secondary outcomes
•
Mortality (neonatal and before discharge)
•
Chronic lung disease (oxygen therapy at 36 weeks'
postmenstrual age)
•
Pneumothorax
•
IVH (all grades) (Papile 1978)
•
Severe IVH (grade III/IV) (Papile 1978)
•
Necrotizing enterocolitis (Bell's ≥ stage 2) (Bell 1978)
•
Sepsis
•
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) (≥ stage 3) (ICCROP 2005)
•
Duration of ETT ventilation (any)
•
Duration of oxygen dependence (days)
•
Duration of hospital stay (days)
•
Nasal septal injury
•
Neurodevelopmental outcome at approximately two years'
corrected age (acceptable range 18 months to 28 months)
including: cerebral palsy, significant mental developmental
delay (e.g. where the patient scores less than 2 standard
deviations (SD) below the mean on standardized testing
such as, but not limited to Bayley Scales of Infant
Development Mental Developmental Index < 70)(Bayley 1993),
legal blindness (< 20/200 visual acuity), and hearing deficit
(aided or < 60 dB on audiometric testing). The composite
outcome “neurodevelopmental impairment” was defined as
having anyone of the aforementioned deficits (modified
from definitions of moderate-to-severe developmental delay)
(Schmidt 2007).
We had intended to examine the outcome patent ductus arteriosus
(PDA). However, this was removed as an outcome as it was not
clinically specified whether authors reported on any PDA or only
treated PDA and, as such, was not clinically relevant. Similarly,
gastric intestinal (GI) perforation is poorly reported on and was also
removed.
Search methods for identification of studies
The Neonatal Group Information Specialist revised the search
strategies for this update to incorporate a more sensitive approach
to NIPPV (nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation) and
NCPAP (nasal CPAP) terminologies; therefore, searches were not
limited by publication year.
Electronic searches
The following databases were searched in January 2023 without
language, publication year, or publication status restrictions:
•
Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials via CRS (Issue 1,
2023)
•
Ovid MEDLINE(R) and Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process, In-Data-
Review & Other Non-Indexed Citations, Daily and Versions <1946
to January 12, 2023>

We searched Epistemonikos (https://www.epistemonikos.org) for
related systematic reviews not identified by database searches. We
checked the reference lists of included studies and the reference
lists of related systematic reviews to identify studies not captured
in database searches. We searched for errata or retractions for
included studies published on PubMed (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
pubmed).
Data collection and analysis
We collected information regarding the method of randomization,
blinding, intervention, stratification, and whether the trial was
single or multicenter for each included study. We noted information
regarding trial participants, as outlined below in Data extraction
and management. We analyzed the clinical outcomes noted above
in Types of outcome measures.
Selection of studies
Results 
were 
screened 
using 
Covidence 
(https://
app.covidence.org). Two authors (MOD, PB) reviewed title/
abstracts and full texts. We resolved any disagreements by
discussion or, when necessary, by a third author (BL).
We recorded the selection process in suficient detail to complete a
PRISMA flow diagram (Moher 2009), and Characteristics of excluded
studies table.
Data extraction and management
Two review authors (MOD, PB) extracted, assessed, and coded
all data for each study, using a form designed specifically for
this review. We piloted the form within the review team using
a sample of included studies. If needed, the standard error of
the mean was replaced by the corresponding standard deviation.
We resolved any disagreements by discussion. One review author
(MOD) entered the final data for each study into Review Manager
Web (RevMan Web 2022), which the other review author (PB)
checked for accuracy. All review authors reviewed the protocol,
analysis, and draf manuscript.
We extracted the following characteristics from each included
study.
•
Administrative details: study author(s); contact details;
published or unpublished; year of publication; the year in which
study was conducted; the presence of vested interest; details of
other relevant papers cited
•
Study: study design; type, duration, and completeness of follow-
up (e.g. greater than 80%); country and location of study;
informed consent; ethics approval
•
Participants: sex; birth weight; gestational age; the number of
participants; inclusion criteria; exclusion criteria, surfactant; use
of flow diagram
•
Interventions: time of initiation, pressures, method of
administration and device used
•
Outcomes as mentioned above under Types of outcome
measures
Assessment of risk of bias in included studies
For this update, three review authors (BL, MOD and PB) assessed
the risk of bias (two authors for each study) using the criteria
outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of
Interventions (Higgins 2017), for the following domains.
• Sequence generation (selection bias)
• Allocation concealment (selection bias)
• Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias)
• Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias)
• Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias)
• Selective reporting (reporting bias)
• Any other bias
We resolved any disagreements by discussion or by a third review
author (BL). See Appendix 7 for a more detailed description of the
risk of bias for each domain.
If needed, we planned to explore the impact of the level of bias by
undertaking sensitivity analyses (see Sensitivity analysis).
Measures of treatment efect
We performed the statistical analyses using: Review Manager
Web (RevMan Web 2022). We summarized the data in a meta-
analysis if they were suficiently homogeneous, both clinically and
statistically.

calculated the number needed to treat for an additional beneficial

Continuous data
For continuous data, we used the mean diference (MD) when
outcomes were measured in the same way between trials. We
planned to use the standardized mean diference (SMD) to
combine trials that measured the same outcome but used diferent
methods. Where trials reported continuous data as the median
and interquartile ranges (IQR), we based our assumptions on the
calculation from Wan 2014. When only ranges were used instead
of SD, we did not estimate the SD as recommended by Cochrane
(Higgins 2022). Similarly, when no SD was available nor additional
information present to allow assumptions of SD, the data were not
included in the analysis.
Unit of analysis issues
The unit of analysis was the participating infant in individually
randomized trials, and an infant was considered only once in the
analysis. We did not identify any cluster-randomized trials.
Dealing with missing data
Where feasible, we intended to carry out analysis on an intention-
to-treat basis for all outcomes. Whenever possible, we analyzed
all participants in the treatment group to which they were
randomized, regardless of the actual treatment received. If we
identified important missing data (in the outcomes) or unclear
data, we requested the missing data by contacting the original
investigators. We made explicit the assumptions of any methods
used to deal with missing data. We performed sensitivity analyses
to assess how sensitive results were to reasonable changes in the
undertaken assumptions. We addressed the potential impact of
missing data on the findings of the review in the Discussion section.
Assessment of heterogeneity
We estimated the treatment efects of individual trials and
examined heterogeneity amongst trials by inspecting the forest
plots and quantifying the impact of heterogeneity using the I2
statistic.
We graded the degree of heterogeneity as: less than 25% no
heterogeneity; 25% to 49% low heterogeneity; 50% to 75%
moderate heterogeneity; more than 75% substantial heterogeneity.
If we noted statistical heterogeneity (I2 > 50%), we explored the
possible causes (e.g. diferences in study quality, participants,
intervention regimens, or outcome assessments).
Assessment of reporting biases
We conducted a comprehensive search for eligible studies and
were alert for duplication of data. As we identified 10 or more
trials for meta-analysis, we assessed possible publication bias by
inspection of a funnel plot. If we uncovered reporting bias that
could, in the opinion of the review authors, introduce serious bias,
we conducted a sensitivity analysis to determine the efect of
including and excluding these studies in the analysis.
Data synthesis
We carried out statistical analysis using Review Manager Web
(RevMan Web 2022). We used the fixed-efect model inverse
variance meta-analysis for combining data where trials examined
the same intervention, and the populations and methods of the
trials were judged to be similar. We assessed the possible source(s)
of heterogeneity using subgroup and sensitivity analysis.
Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity
We explored high statistical heterogeneity in the outcomes by
visually inspecting the forest plots and by removing the outlying
studies in the sensitivity analysis. Where statistical heterogeneity
was significant, we interpreted the results of the meta-analyses
accordingly.

Sensitivity analysis
We planned sensitivity analyses on the primary outcome to
determine how estimates were afected by including only studies

•
Mortality (neonatal and before discharge);

at 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age;

Included studies
We identified 17 studies (seven new studies for this update) that
met our inclusion criteria (Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2014; Armanian
2019; Bisceglia 2007; Dursun 2019; Farhat 2018; Gharehbaghi 2019;
Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007; Lista 2009; Meneses
2011; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021; Ramanathan 2012; Salama 2015; Wood
2013). Please see the Characteristics of included studies table.
Fifeen studies were randomized trials (Aguiar 2015; Armanian
2019; Bisceglia 2007; Dursun 2019; Farhat 2018; Gharehbaghi 2019;
Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007; Lista 2009; Meneses
2011; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021; Ramanathan 2012; Wood 2013), and
two were quasi-randomized (Armanian 2014; Salama 2015).
All studies enrolled infants with respiratory distress requiring
respiratory support in their first six hours; however, in eight studies,
respiratory distress syndrome was well-defined with radiological
criteria (Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019; Bisceglia 2007; Dursun
2019 ; Lista 2009; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021; Salama 2015), while in
nine studies, infants at risk of respiratory distress syndrome (no
chest radiograph required) were enrolled (Aguiar 2015; Farhat 2018;
Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007;
Meneses 2011; Ramanathan 2012; Wood 2013). In three studies,
infants received surfactant via the INSURE method (Intubate-
Surfactant-Extubate) prior to randomization (Lista 2009; Pan 2021;
Ramanathan 2012); in five studies, infants did not receive surfactant
before randomization (Armanian 2014; Bisceglia 2007; Kugelman
2007; Meneses 2011; Wood 2013); and in nine studies, some
infants received surfactant before randomization while others
did not (Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2019; Dursun 2019; Farhat 2018;
Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009; Oncel 2016;
Salama 2015). Only one study used minimally invasive surfactant
therapy (MIST) (Oncel 2016). Six studies did not mandate infants
to receive cafeine or a methylxanthine prior to randomization
(Bisceglia 2007; Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007; Lista
2009; Salama 2015). This was unclear in one study (Wood 2013).
Population
Eight studies included infants born at 32 weeks' gestation or
less (Aguiar 2015; Dursun 2019; Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013;
Meneses 2011; Oncel 2016; Ramanathan 2012; Wood 2013). Other
trials included infants born up to 34 weeks (Bisceglia 2007; Farhat
2018; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007; Lista 2009; Salama 2015;
Armanian 2014) or less than 1500 g (Armanian 2019; Pan 2021). Only
five trials included infants born at less than 28 weeks (Kirpalani
2013; Kugelman 2007; Meneses 2011; Oncel 2016; Ramanathan
2012).
Interventions
All studies compared NIPPV to NCPAP, with two studies having
a third comparison (heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula)
(Armanian 2019; Farhat 2018).
Eleven trials used NIPPV delivered via ventilator (Armanian
2014; Armanian 2019; Bisceglia 2007; Dursun 2019; Farhat 2018;
Gharehbaghi 2019; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007; Meneses 2011;
Oncel 2016; Salama 2015), four used bilevel devices (Aguiar 2015;
Lista 2009; Pan 2021; Wood 2013), and two used both ventilator-
driven and bilevel devices (Kirpalani 2013; Ramanathan 2012).
Six studies used synchronized NIPPV (Dursun 2019; Gharehbaghi
2019; Kugelman 2007; Lista 2009; Salama 2015; Wood 2013),
and 10 did not (Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019;
Bisceglia 2007; Farhat 2018; Kishore 2009; Meneses 2011; Oncel
2016; Pan 2021; Ramanathan 2012). One pragmatic study used both
synchronous and non-synchronous devices, which we have termed
'mixed devices' (Kirpalani 2013).
Levels of CPAP used in the studies varied, but generally were 5 to 6
cm H20 (with three studies allowing up to 7 or 8). For studies using
NIPPV delivered via a ventilator, the settings varied, but generally,
the PIP was 15 to 20 cm H20. For studies using a bilevel device,
the PIP was generally 8 to 10 cm H20. No study matched the mean
airway pressure between the intervention and control groups.
Excluded studies
We excluded 54 studies (see Characteristics of excluded studies), for
the following reasons:
•
Studies that evaluated infants with apnea included Bai 2014;
Beaullieu 2019; Gizzi 2015; Lin 1998; Lin 2011; Pantalitschka 2009
and Ryan 1989.
•
Studies that evaluated infants afer extubation included Abyar
2011; Barrington 2001; El-Farrash 2021; Estay 2020; Friedlich
1999; Gao 2010; Jasani 2016; Kahramaner 2014; Khalaf 2001;
Khorana 2008; Komatsu 2016; Li 2021; Manjunatha 2019; Migliori
2005; Moretti 2008; Najafian 2019; O'Brien 2012; Ribeiro 2017;
Victor 2016 and Yllescas-Medrano 2004.
•
Studies that were not RCTs (or quasi-randomized trials)
included Aghai 2006; Askari 2018; Herber-Jonat 2006; Liu 2003;
Manzar 2004; Migliori 2005; Ryan 1989; Skariah 2019 and
CTRI/2018/01/011116.
•
Studies where randomization occurred afer six hours post-birth
included Chen 2013; Gao 2014; and Lee 2020.
•
Studies comparing synchronized NIPPV versus mechanical
ventilation included Bhandari 2007; and Ramanathan 2009.
•
Studies where there was no report on the primary outcome
included Baneshi 2014; and Yuan 2021.
•
Studies which enrolled twins only included Chen 2015.
•
Studies which compared high-flow nasal cannula versus NIPPV
included Kugelman 2014a.
•
Studies which compared two devices/methods of providing
NIPPV or CPAP included Bober 2012; and Salvo 2015.
•
Studies which compared NIPPV versus conventional ventilation
included Santin 2004.
•
Studies that included term infants included Shi 2010; and Shi
2014.
•
Studies that examined the efect of DuoPAP (Hamilton Medical,
Bonaduz, Switzerland) included Kong 2012; Malakian 2021; and
Zhou 2015.
•
Studies where NIPPV and CPAP were used early as a primary
mode of support and also post-extubation included Silveira
2015.
•
Studies where nonrandomized data were re-evaluated from a
previous study that was already included in this review (Millar
2016).
•
Studies using additional Chinese traditional medicine as an
adjunct included Lv 2020.

Allocation
Random sequence generation: 12 of the included trials met this
criterion. This was unclear in three trials (Farhat 2018; Gharehbaghi
2019; Wood 2013), and considered high-risk in two trials (Armanian
2014; Salama 2015).
Allocation concealment: this was adequate in 11 trials and unclear
in six (Armanian 2014; Bisceglia 2007; Farhat 2018; Gharehbaghi
2019; Salama 2015; Wood 2013).
Blinding
Given the nature of the intervention, it was deemed that none of the
studies could blind the participants, personnel. It also was not clear
whether outcome assessment was blinded or not for most studies.
Incomplete outcome data
Fourteen trials showed a low risk for attrition bias while three
trials were deemed as unclear (Farhat 2018; Salama 2015; Wood
2013). Given the lack of clarity towards attrition, rather than clear
loss of participants, we used the data without making further
assumptions. These studies were generally found to be of lower
quality for which a sensitivity analysis was later performed.
Selective reporting
Selective reporting was graded as low risk in 11 trials, while five
were deemed unclear (Armanian 2014; Bisceglia 2007; Farhat 2018;
Salama 2015; Wood 2013). One trial was deemed as high-risk
(Armanian 2019).
Other potential sources of bias
Other sources of bias were present in seven trials, where four were
unclear (Bisceglia 2007; Dursun 2019; Ramanathan 2012; Wood
2013), and three were deemed high-risk (Aguiar 2015; Farhat 2018;
Salama 2015).

Primary outcome
Respiratory failure: defined by respiratory acidosis, increased oxygen
requirement, or apnea that was frequent or severe, leading to
additional ventilatory support during the first week of life (Outcome
1.1)
All studies reported the primary outcomes clearly, except for two
studies (Farhat 2018; Pan 2021), which only reported percentages
(absolute number of events derived from the percentage), for which
we presumed that all the infants were reported on. When compared
to CPAP, NIPPV likely reduces rates of respiratory failure in the first
week of life in infants (risk ratio (RR) 0.65, 95% confidence interval
(CI) 0.54 to 0.78; risk diference (RD) -0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.05;
1958 infants; I2 of 0%; moderate-certainty evidence; Analysis 1.1;
Figure 4), with 13 infants (95% CI 8 to 20) needing to be treated
with NIPPV to prevent one respiratory failure. This included the
infants who sustained respiratory failure requiring endotracheal
tube ventilation and the infants who had respiratory failure but
were rescued using an alternative mode of noninvasive ventilation
upon deterioration (i.e. CPAP to NIPPV). The efect on respiratory
failure was observed in all populations, regardless of whether
surfactant was received before randomization or not.

Owing to methodological limitations (risk of bias in all categories
assessed) in three studies (Farhat 2018; Salama 2015; Wood 2013),
we performed a post hoc sensitivity analysis for the outcome of
respiratory failure, including the 14 higher-quality studies (Aguiar
2015; Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019; Bisceglia 2007; Dursun 2019;
Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007;

2012). Results were similar (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.74; RD -0.09,
95% CI -0.13 to -0.06).
We analyzed the funnel plot for this outcome and noted a certain
asymmetry where small trials favoring NIPPV may not have been
published(Figure 5). This suggests a potential reporting bias. As
such, it is possible that we are currently underestimating the true
efect of the intervention.

Only the mixed population studies (Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2019;
Dursun 2019; Farhat 2018; Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013;
Kishore 2009; Oncel 2016; Salama 2015) showed that NIPPV likely
reduces endotracheal intubation compared to CPAP (RR 0.62, 95%

receiving surfactant or no surfactant before enrollment had fewer
studies reporting this outcome. They showed a similar trend, but
the efect was smaller, and the confidence intervals were wider,
leading to NIPPV likely resulting in little to no diference in the need
for endotracheal tube ventilation.
The funnel plot for this outcome showed an asymmetry where
small trials favoring NIPPV may not have been published (Figure 7).
This suggests a potential reporting bias. As such, it is possible that
we are currently underestimating the true efect of the intervention.

Eleven studies reported this outcome (Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2014;
Armanian 2019; Farhat 2018; Kishore 2009; Kugelman 2007; Lista
2009; Meneses 2011; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021; Ramanathan 2012), with
five studies reporting data in a way that precluded meta-analysis
(missing values or using ranges - Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019;
Farhat 2018; Kugelman 2007; Oncel 2016). These studies showed a
high degree of heterogeneity (I2 of 82%). Only three studies (Lista
2009; Pan 2021; Ramanathan 2012), demonstrated a reduction in
the number of days on oxygen amongst infants who received NIPPV;
all are studies where infants received surfactant before enrollment.
We graded the evidence for this outcome as very low-certainty.
Duration of endotracheal tube intubation
Seven studies reported this outcome, but three studies reported
data in a way that precluded meta-analysis (i.e. missing values,
using ranges - Farhat 2018; Oncel 2016; Ramanathan 2012).
Duration of intubation and mechanical ventilation varied between
trials, with one trial reporting a mean duration of 7 to 12 hours
(Bisceglia 2007), and two other trials reporting a mean duration
between 10 and 13 days (Kugelman 2007; Meneses 2011). This
heterogeneity precluded a meaningful meta-analysis. Overall, no
trial reported a reduction in the time required for mechanical
ventilation in infants who received NIPPV. We graded the evidence
for this outcome as very low-certainty.
Upper airway injury
Kishore 2009 reported two infants in each group with local upper
airway injury. The study authors did not specify the nature of the
injury and did not state whether it was a nasal septal injury. Salama
2015 reported 20 cases of nasal injury in the NCPAP group (out of 30
infants) and none in the NIPPV group, without further description.
We graded the evidence for this outcome as very low-certainty.
NIPPV versus NCPAP (by device) (Comparison 2)
Ventilator-generated NIPPV likely reduces the rate of respiratory
failure compared to CPAP (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.78; 1131
infants; moderate-certainty evidence; Analysis 2.1). This may be
confounded by synchronization. Bilevel-generated NIPPV probably
results in little to no diference in respiratory failure, however,
fewer studies were available (Aguiar 2015; Lista 2009; Pan 2021;
Wood 2013), and wide confidence intervals were present. When
mixed devices were used, NIPPV likely reduces respiratory failures
compared to CPAP (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.85; 163 infants;
moderate-certainty evidence) though only two studies were
available (Kirpalani 2013; Ramanathan 2012), and wide confidence
intervals were present. The study authors provided no information
on the relative proportion of infants who received NIPPV via
ventilator or bilevel device (Analysis 2.1).
Owing to methodological limitations (risk of bias in all categories
assessed) in three studies (Farhat 2018; Salama 2015; Wood 2013),
we performed a post hoc sensitivity analysis for the outcome of
respiratory failure, including only the 14 higher-quality studies
(Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019; Bisceglia 2007;
Dursun 2019; Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009;
Kugelman 2007; Lista 2009; Meneses 2011; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021;
Ramanathan 2012). Results were largely unchanged.
Similarly, NIPPV via ventilator likely reduces the need for intubation
in comparison to CPAP (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.79; RD -0.10, 95%
CI -0.14 to -0.05; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial
outcome (NNTB) 10 (95% CI 7 to 20); 1131 infants; Analysis 2.2).
Alternatively, infants who received NIPPV via bilevel device likely
experience little to no diference in the rate of intubation compared
to CPAP (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.18; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.08 to
0.02; 664 infants). Mixed devices' delivery of NIPPV likely reduces
the need for endotracheal intubation (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.85;
RD -0.16, 95% CI -0.27 to -0.04; 163 infants) but only two studies
were available.
Examination of CLD by the type of device delivering NIPPV showed
that ventilator-generated NIPPV may reduce CLD rates (RR 0.65,
95% CI 0.45 to 0.94, RD -0.06, 95% CI -0.10 to -0.01; number needed
to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) 17 (95% CI 10
to 100); 741 infants; Analysis 2.4). The bilevel (Aguiar 2015; Lista
2009; Wood 2013) and mixed devices subgroups (Kirpalani 2013;
Ramanathan 2012), delivering NIPPV suggest that NIPPV results in
little to no diference in CLD, though only two studies were available
for each group. The evidence suggests that NIPPV results in little to
no diference in the rate of mortality (Analysis 2.3), pneumothoraces
(Analysis 2.5), or severe IVH when compared to CPAP (Analysis 2.6).
Synchronized versus non-synchronized NIPPV (Comparison 3)
Non-synchronized NIPPV and synchronized NIPPV likely reduce
respiratory failure compared to CPAP (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.81;
1456 infants; moderate-certainty evidence for non-synchronized
NIPPV; RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.89; 449 infants; moderate-certainty
evidence for synchronized NIPPV). Non-synchronized NIPPV (RR
0.66, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.81; 1546 infants) and synchronized NIPPV (RR
0.62, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.91; 449 infants; Analysis 3.2), likely reduces
the need for intubation.
Owing to methodological limitations (risk of bias in all categories
assessed) in three studies (Farhat 2018; Salama 2015; Wood
2013), we performed a post hoc sensitivity analysis for the
outcome of respiratory failure, including only the 14 higher-quality
studies (Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019; Bisceglia
2007; Dursun 2019; Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013; Kishore

NIPPV versus CPAP in various socioeconomic status based on
the country of the study (Comparison 4)
We evaluated all the studies from this review based on the
socioeconomic status of the study's country of origin. In high-
income economies (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.88; 715 infants)
and upper middle-income economies (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.44 to
0.77; 768 infants), NIPPV likely reduces the rate of respiratory
failure in comparison to CPAP. In contrast, in lower middle-income
economies (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.13; 475 infants), the use of
NIPPV likely results in little to no diference in the rate of respiratory
failure (reduced efect size and increased confidence Interval)
(Analysis 4.1). The need for intubation outcome yields somewhat
similar trends when stratified by economic status (Analysis 4.2), yet
high-income economies overlap 1.0 (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.03;
605 infants). The use of NIPPV in various economies may result in
little to no diference in CLD but, in the high-income economies, the
confidence interval was just below 1 (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.99;
715 infants; Analysis 4.4). Similarly, the economic status had no
impact on the incidence of pneumothorax (Analysis 4.5), and severe
IVH (Analysis 4.6). While we could not conclude on the outcome
of mortality, the absolute number of events was lower in high-
income economies (Analysis 4.3 - 21/231 and 29/244 for NIPPV and
CPAP, respectively, in lower middle-income economies, 45/386 and
50/382 for NIPPV and CPAP, respectively, in upper middle-income
economies, and 3/352 and 6/379 for NIPPV and CPAP, respectively,
in high-income economies).
Owing to methodological limitations (risk of selection and
reporting bias) in three studies (Farhat 2018; Salama 2015; Wood
2013), we performed a post hoc sensitivity analysis for the outcome
of respiratory failure, including only the 14 higher-quality studies
(Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019; Bisceglia 2007;
Dursun 2019; Gharehbaghi 2019; Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009;
Kugelman 2007; Lista 2009; Meneses 2011; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021;
Ramanathan 2012). The lower-quality studies were primarily found
in the lower middle-income economies group. Their removal did
not change the outcome between the groups.
Post hoc comparison: NIPPV versus CPAP and respiratory
failure up to 72 hours or up to 7 days (Comparison 5)
We performed a post hoc analysis examining the efect of NIPPV
and CPAP on the outcome of respiratory failure at 72 hours versus
seven days. Ten studies reported this outcome by 72 hours post-
randomization (Armanian 2014; Armanian 2019; Bisceglia 2007;
Dursun 2019; Farhat 2018; Gharehbaghi 2019; Meneses 2011;
Oncel 2016; Pan 2021; Wood 2013), while four studies reported
this outcome within seven days post-randomization (Aguiar 2015;
Kirpalani 2013; Kishore 2009; Ramanathan 2012). In three studies,
the timing of reporting for this outcome was unclear (Kugelman
2007; Lista 2009; Salama 2015). NIPPV likely reduces the rate of
respiratory failure whether determined over the first 72 hours post-
randomization (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89; 1315 infants) or the
first week (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.82; 459 infants) when compared
to CPAP. The removal of lower-quality studies (Farhat 2018; Wood
2013), did not change the results of the outcomes.
Other planned post hoc comparisons
We could not perform subgroup analyses based on baseline
characteristics of participants (e.g. infants weighing less than 1000
grams or corrected age at the time of intervention e.g. infants less
than 28 weeks' gestation), as all studies had a mean gestational age
of around 30 weeks. Only two studies included infants with a mean
gestational age of 28 weeks.
D I S C U S S I O N
Summary of main results
In comparison to CPAP, nasal intermittent positive pressure
ventilation (NIPPV) may reduce respiratory failure or the need for
intubation in the first few days afer birth in preterm infants at
risk or with respiratory distress syndrome when applied within six
hours of birth. Compared to the previous iteration of this review, we
identified that NIPPV may reduce the risk of chronic lung disease
slightly. We identified no other short-term benefits or harms. We
also evaluated the impact of socioeconomic status by country of
income on these outcomes. We noted that socioeconomic status
may influence the degree of benefit of the NIPPV intervention.
Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
It is reasonable to conclude that NIPPV is likely more efective
than NCPAP in providing respiratory support to preterm infants
and in preventing the need for intubation when applied within
the first six hours afer birth. It is important to note that the
studies included in this review enrolled infants who were either at
risk of respiratory distress syndrome, while others had respiratory
distress syndrome. This may represent a heterogenous population
with infants receiving the intervention in a preventive manner (at-
risk infants) while others in a therapeutic manner (infants with
diagnosed RDS). However, given the variability in the description
of respiratory distress and the dificulty in identifying those at
risk who may subsequently have developed respiratory distress
syndrome, we could not properly assess the diference in primary
intent of treatment (i.e. prevention vs therapeutic administration
of NIPPV vs CPAP) and its efectiveness when used in these
contexts. However, this remains an interesting question that should
be examined in future research and data synthesis of future
systematic reviews. When considering other subgroup analyses,
results may have revealed diferences in the efectiveness of
diferent devices used to provide NIPPV (ventilator and bilevel).
Ventilator-driven devices appear superior to bilevel devices in
providing NIPPV. This diference may be due to the higher mean
airway pressures generated by the ventilator. However, additional
studies are needed to confirm this. Synchronization of the device
did not appear to ofer advantages over non-synchronized delivery
in the studies included.
We did find evidence of a diferential efect of the study setting
(high versus low income). We note a discrepancy between high-
and low-income economies where NIPPV benefits are not present in
lower middle-income economies. As such, the findings of this study

may not be applicable globally. To note, absolute data for mortality
was drastically higher amongst low-income economies compared
to high-income economies.
We note that researchers should further assess benefits and
relatively uncommon risks such as pneumothorax and severe
intraventricular hemorrhage because occasionally large trials
can disagree with the results of the meta-analysis of smaller
trials (Cappelleri 1996; Villar 1995). Multiple small trials were
identified in this update, most originating from lower middle-
income economies. Hence, the findings should be interpreted with
this in mind. We did not appreciate a considerable variability
in the mean GA of enrollment amongst studies included in this
iteration. Most trials enrolled infants with a gestational age of
approximately 28 to 32 weeks with an overall mean gestational
age of around 30 weeks. As such, the results of this review may
not apply to extremely preterm infants that are most at risk of
needing mechanical ventilation or developing CLD. The lack of data
available for this group of infants is a major limitation. The clinician
taking care of extremely preterm infants should be wary that no
concrete data are available at the moment for this group. In fact,
it is reasonable to think that the extremely preterm infant may
be at higher risk of failure of noninvasive ventilation compared to
less preterm infants leading to an increased frequency of traumatic
intubation. A recent study showed that only 24-64% of intubation
is successful on the first attempt, which depends on the level of
experience of the provider (Foglia 2019).
In this review, we continued to make the distinction between
respiratory failure and need for endotracheal intubation. This is
important yet subtle, as respiratory failure includes both patients
who were escalated from CPAP to NIPPV or to mechanical
ventilation. While this review did not show a major diference in
the outcomes, we continue to expect that researchers may attempt
to limit mechanical ventilation exposure by using NIPPV or other
noninvasive methods more frequently as a rescue option.
A newly available method (noninvasive neurally adjusted
ventilatory assist, or NAVA) has shown promise in small case
series (Lee 2015; Lee 2019; Stein 2012), but further assessment
with properly powered randomized trials is needed. Similarly, new
strategies to administer surfactant, such as minimally invasive
surfactant therapy (MIST)/less invasive surfactant administration
(LISA), may ofer an added benefit in limiting exposure to
mechanical ventilation. Only one of the included studies used
such a technique (Oncel 2016). However, the usage of MIST/LISA is
likely now the predominant method in surfactant administration
(over INSURE). As such, the studies included may not represent
current practices and this highlights a need for further research,
including trials akin to current practices (with LISA as a surfactant
administration method).
Quality of the evidence
Most included studies were small, single-center trials. Three of
the 17 trials identified in this review had major methodological
limitations. One trial was quasi-randomized and had a potential
selection and reporting bias (Salama 2015). One further trial had
an unclear or high risk of selection bias and reporting bias (Farhat
2018). The third trial relied on abstract findings from 2013, for
which the manuscript remains unpublished (Wood 2013). Because
of the nature of the interventions, it has been impossible to blind
caregivers, and bias may have arisen through the uneven use of
co-interventions. To note, nine studies had at least one area that
may lead to potential bias (not considering blinding, as discussed
above); seven of the studies appeared free of other potential bias
(Kishore 2009; Kirpalani 2013; Kugelman 2007; Lista 2009; Meneses
2011; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021). Investigators dealt with potential
confounders, such as methylxanthine usage and indications for
intubation, by having management protocols in place and by using
objective respiratory failure criteria, enhancing confidence in study
findings. Trials without such stringent definitions are awaiting
further clarifications. Many studies did not appropriately define
some of their secondary outcomes (CLD, NEC, ROP, etc.) or used
diferent definitions than the ones specified in the review protocol.
Hence, the results for these outcomes were not included in our
analysis.
Potential biases in the review process
Potential biases could have been introduced in the review process
based on decisions made at various levels. Our criteria for inclusion
of preterm infants encompassed all infants below 37 weeks of
gestational age. While this ofers thorough inclusion of participants,
this may not solely target the infants for whom noninvasive
ventilation is most beneficial in the current neonatology landscape.
For example, late premature infants may not be the population
most at risk of respiratory failure, need for intubation, and
consequent chronic lung disease, which may positively afect the
outcomes of this study. Furthermore, the limitation introduced on
the timing of the intervention (i.e. within six hours) may not be
representative of real-world practices where the intervention can
be introduced when it is felt necessary based on clinical findings. It
is plausible that the introduction of the intervention at a later time
may not yield a similar result as it may be reactive to the clinical
situation rather than in a preventative manner. In fact, the review
included both patients that were at risk of respiratory distress
syndrome as well as patients with respiratory distress syndrome,
which calls attention to the issue that some patients received the
intervention in a preventative context while others in a therapeutic
context. This distinction may be important and will require further
attention in the future. Similarly, wider inclusion criteria about the
timing of implementation (sequentially, i.e. 0 to 6 hours, 6 to 12
hours, 12 to 24 hours, 24 hours and beyond) of the intervention
will be helpful to match current practice and identify whether the
benefit of NIPPV extends beyond six hours afer birth. NAVA-NIPPV
was not included within the review process of systematic review
but may have added additional infants to the review, strengthening
the results obtained. This new mode of synchronization may prove
beneficial and should be considered in future.
We placed nine studies (Cetinkaya 2018; Esmaeilnia 2016; Fu 2014;
Gomez 2017; Öktem 2021; Ozdemir 2016; Ozdemir 2017; Sabzehei
2018; Sadeghnia 2016), in the awaiting classification category due
to a lack of information about the definition of the primary outcome
(+/- secondary outcomes) or time frame used to reach the primary
outcome (Esmaeilnia 2016; Fu 2014; Öktem 2021; Sabzehei 2018;
Sadeghnia 2016) or the gestational age of the infants (Gomez
2017). We attempted to reach the primary author for clarification.
Other studies had results that were in an abstract format without
enough information to draw conclusions, with expectations of
published studies in the future (Cetinkaya 2018; Ozdemir 2016;
Ozdemir 2017). Two studies had no information on the time of
initiation of the intervention (Esmaeilnia 2016; Öktem 2021). Two
additional studies (for a total of 11) were placed in the awaiting

Agreements and disagreements with other studies or
reviews
Ramaswamy 2020 compared the efectiveness of multiple
noninvasive ventilation strategies for preterm infants with RDS. In
contrast to our review, high-flow nasal cannula was included, while
NIPPV and BiPAP were considered diferent. As such, studies that
included NIPPV and BiPAP as a single intervention were excluded.
Additionally, the implementation of the intervention was within
24 hours of life (rather than six hours of life). As such, additional
references were added due to the less restrictive inclusion
parameters. With respect to our primary outcomes of respiratory
failure and the need for intubation, comparable results were
obtained. Unlike the results obtained in our review, the authors
found that NIPPV confers a decreased risk of pneumothorax and
mortality compared to CPAP.
Solevåg 2021 performed a systematic review of noninvasive
ventilation for infants with RDS. They included the use of
noninvasive ventilation both for primary respiratory support
and post-extubation. In contrast with our review, the primary
outcomes were bronchopulmonary dysplasia and mortality, while
noninvasive ventilation failure was a secondary outcome. These
diferent primary outcomes explain the diferences in the included
studies. Fewer studies were included by Solevåg than in this
review (8 versus 17 studies in this review, 1172 infants versus
1958 infants in this review). The inclusion criteria were also
more restrictive (only English studies and published data were
included). The outcome definitions were not clearly defined, which
increased heterogeneity. Nevertheless, comparable results were
obtained. Both reported a reduction in noninvasive ventilation
failure, reduced rates of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and little
to no diference in mortality in the NIPPV group compared to
the NCPAP group. Subgroup analyses based on synchronization
(synchronized vs non-synchronized) and mode of generation
of the NIPPV/BiPAP (ventilator or BiPAP) were not performed.
Rather, synchronized NIPPV and BiPAP were directly compared to
NCPAP separately without considering non-synchronized NIPPV.
Therefore, we cannot directly compare subanalyses undertaken in
the two reviews.
The systematic review of Ruegger 2021 included very similar
studies. However, we classified two of them amongst awaiting
classification in the hope to have further clarification before
inclusion (Sabzehei 2018; Sadeghnia 2016) and we excluded
two (Kong 2012; Skariah 2019), while three studies (Armanian
2019; Farhat 2018; Pan 2021) were not included in their
review. Nevertheless, their study produced similar results to
our review. However, their data compilation difered from ours
as they subdivided the infants into four subgroups based
on the style of ventilation received: synchronized ventilator-
generated NIPPV, non-synchronized ventilator-generated NIPPV,
synchronized flow-driver-generated NIPPV, and non-synchronized
flow-driver-generated NIPPV. This further refined the intervention
beyond our review but may help the clinician better appreciate
specific situations.
A U T H O R S '   C O N C L U S I O N S
Implications for practice
When applied within six hours afer birth, NIPPV likely reduces
the risk of respiratory failure and the need for intubation and
endotracheal tube ventilation for the treatment of very preterm
infants (GA 28 weeks and above) with respiratory distress syndrome
or at risk for RDS. It may also decrease the rate of CLD slightly.
However, most trials enrolled infants with a gestational age of
approximately 28 to 32 weeks with an overall mean gestational age
of around 30 weeks. As such, the results of this review may not
apply to extremely preterm infants that are most at risk of needing
mechanical ventilation or developing CLD. Further well-powered
studies are needed to confirm these results and to assess the safety
of NIPPV compared with NCPAP.
Implications for research
Future research should assess the eficacy and safety of early
NIPPV compared with NCPAP for the treatment of extremely
preterm infants with RDS (e.g. born before 28 weeks gestation).
These patients are at the highest risk of mechanical ventilation,
prolonged time on a ventilator with subsequent development
of CLD. Other areas of interest include the diference between
devices used for delivery, their synchronization as well as the intent
of treatment (preventative vs therapeutic). Attempts at matching
similar mean airway pressure between ventilation modes should
be addressed to decipher the underlying mechanism leading to the
beneficial efect. Additionally, future updates of this review should
consider the inclusion of infants beyond six hours of age, up to 24
hours afer birth to provide data on NIPPV efect in a multitude
of diferent scenarios reciprocating real-life situations. Clinically
relevant outcomes, such as long-term survival and incidence of
neurodevelopmental impairment, are important to explore and
should be sought in future research. Neurally adjusted ventilatory
assist or noninvasive NAVA needs further assessment with properly
powered randomized trials.

Methods

Funding: section of Neonatology of the Portuguese Society of Paediatrics (Abbott grant)

chromosomal abnormality, neuromuscular disease

Incidence of intrusive mechanical ventilation; the incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia

Study name
NCPAP + MISA vs. NIPPV + MISA to NRDS: a multicenter randomized study
Methods
Study design: the study was a multicenter, randomized, clinical, parallel-group study
Setting: 16 level III neonatal intensive care units in China
Duration of study: 1 December 2021, and 30 August 2023
Participants
Inclusion criteria: participants enrolled: spontaneously breathing preterm infants born between
24 and 29.9 weeks' gestational age with signs of respiratory distress syndrome. Preterm infants
were receiving nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) or noninvasive positive pressure
ventilation (NIPPV) without intubation before surfactant administration. Patients diagnosed with
NRDS on noninvasive respiratory support (NIPPV or NCPAP) were given a therapeutic dose of pul-
monary surfactant via MISA within 120 minutes after birth. Parental consent was obtained for all
participants before birth.
Exclusion criteria
(1) Preterm infants who had been intubated prior to pulmonary surfactant administration due to
postnatal resuscitation or other reasons
(2) Preterm infants with obvious malformations
(3) Newborns who died or were transferred to other hospitals for surgery or whose information was
incomplete
(4) Infants who participated in other interventional research projects
Number randomized: 960
Interventions
NCPAP settings: PEEP 6 cm H2O (adjustment range 6 - 8cm H2O), FiO2 adjustment range 0.21-0.40,
in order to achieve postnatal target oxygen saturation.

Appendix 7. Risk of bias tool
The following issues were evaluated and entered into the risk of bias table:
1. Sequence generation (checking for possible selection bias). Was the allocation sequence adequately generated?
For each included study, we categorized the method used to generate the allocation sequence as:
a. low risk (any truly random process, eg, random number table, computer random number generator);
b. high risk (any nonrandom process, eg, odd or even date of birth, hospital or clinic record number); or
c. unclear risk.
2. Allocation concealment (checking for possible selection bias). Was allocation adequately concealed?

For each included study, we categorized the method used to conceal the allocation sequence as:
a. low risk (eg, telephone or central randomization, consecutively numbered sealed opaque envelopes);
b. high risk (open random allocation, eg, unsealed or nonopaque envelopes, alternation, date of birth); or
c. unclear risk.
3. Blinding (checking for possible performance bias). Was knowledge of the allocated intervention adequately prevented during the study?
At study entry? At the time of outcome assessment?
For each included study, we categorized the methods used to blind study participants and personnel from knowledge of which intervention
a participant received. Blinding was assessed separately for diferent outcomes or classes of outcomes. We categorized the methods as:
a. low risk, high risk or unclear risk for participants;
b. low risk, high risk or unclear risk for personnel; or
c. low risk, high risk or unclear risk for outcome assessors.
4. Incomplete outcome data (checking for possible attrition bias through withdrawals, dropouts, protocol deviations). Were incomplete
outcome data adequately addressed?
For each included study and for each outcome, we described the completeness of data including attrition and exclusions from the analysis.
We noted whether attrition and exclusions were reported, the numbers included in the analysis at each stage (compared with the total
randomized participants), reasons for attrition or exclusion when reported, and whether missing data were balanced across groups or were
related to outcomes. When suficient information was reported or supplied by trial authors, we re-included missing data in the analyses.
We categorized the methods as:
a. low risk (< 20% missing data);
b. high risk (≥ 20% missing data); or
c. unclear risk.
5. Selective reporting bias. Are reports of the study free of suggestion of selective outcome reporting?
For each included study, we described how we investigated the possibility of selective outcome reporting bias and what we found. We
assessed the methods as:
a. low risk (when it is clear that all of the study’s prespecified outcomes and all expected outcomes of interest to the review have been
reported);
b. high risk (when not all of the study’s prespecified outcomes have been reported; one or more reported primary outcomes were not
prespecified; outcomes of interest were reported incompletely and so cannot be used; study failed to include results of a key outcome that
would have been expected to have been reported); or
c. unclear risk.
6. Other sources of bias. Was the study apparently free of other problems that could put it at high risk of bias?
For each included study, we described any important concerns that we had about other possible sources of bias (eg, whether a potential
source of bias was related to the specific study design, whether the trial was stopped early owing to some data-dependent process). We
assessed whether each study was free of other problems that could put it at risk of bias as:
a. low risk;
b. high risk; or
c. unclear risk.
If needed, we planned to explore the impact of the level of bias by undertaking sensitivity analyses.

We identified seven new trials (Aguiar 2015; Armanian 2019; Dur-
sun 2019; Farhat 2018; Gharehbaghi 2019; Oncel 2016; Pan 2021).
The review reaffirmed that NIPPV likely reduces the rate of respi-
ratory failure and re-intubation compared to CPAP in infants at
risk or with respiratory distress syndrome. This updated review
showed that NIPPV may reduce rates of CLD slightly compared to
CPAP, which was previously not demonstrated in the previous it-
eration of this review.

D I F F E R E N C E S   B E T W E E N   P R O T O C O L   A N D   R E V I E W
For this update, a few changes have been made to the protocol of previous updates of this review:
•
We omitted CINAHL from the database search.
•
We updated methods and reporting based on the current template for Cochrane Neonatal reviews.
•
We removed patent ductus arteriosus as a secondary outcome as this is not an uncommon event in this population in the postnatal
period and does not ofer additional information on the intervention.
•
We used a method to derive mean and SD for continuous outcomes when only median and interquartile ranges were available (Wan
2014).
•
We added a subgroup analysis based on the economic status of the country of origin of the study.
